title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Presentation and Q&A at the Boston College on October 9, 2014
summary: Pabrai presents 'Cloning 101', explaining how Pabrai Funds, Dakshana and his new Dhandho Holdings insurance vehicle are all cloned from Buffett and Munger, and contrasts negotiated markets like Iowa farmland with auction-driven stock markets that swing wildly. In the Q&A he shares lessons from his lunch with Buffett (inner scorecard, Rick Guerin and patience), his filtering process for ideas, the 2x-in-2-years hurdle, circle of competence, a live valuation of Jammu and Kashmir Bank, and why secular-decline retailers like Sears are traps.

ideas.idea: Cloning the Buffett partnership structure (no management fee, performance fee only, annual reporting, no holdings disclosure) is itself a competitive advantage because almost nobody else does it.
ideas.detail: He started Pabrai Funds in 1999, 30 years after Buffett closed his partnership, and found no one had replicated the structure; 15 years later the share of funds using it is still a rounding error, less than 1%.

ideas.idea: Nonprofits should swing for the fences: focus on one or two causes and concentrate endowment assets, even 90%+ in one stock, as Munger advises.
ideas.detail: Dakshana cloned the Bihar 'Super 30' IIT coaching model and follows Buffett/Munger principles; because he and his wife give 2% of net worth each year, a total loss in one year would not terminate the foundation.

ideas.idea: Dhandho Holdings clones the Berkshire/Fairfax/Markel model of buying insurance companies, leaving the operators alone and taking over the investment side, because almost none of the 3,000 US P&C insurers do this.
ideas.detail: He raised about $150 million in Q1 2014, agreed to acquire a private insurer, and intends a permanent-capital, never-sell vehicle; the US P&C industry takes in about $550 billion of premiums a year but good underwriters almost never have investment skill, so finding and freeing a 'Lou Simpson' is the rare edge.

ideas.idea: Negotiated markets between intelligent buyers and sellers of productive assets, like Iowa farmland, produce smooth, rational prices; stock markets are auction-driven and therefore swing wildly, which is the value investor's opportunity.
ideas.detail: Iowa farmland went from about $5,000/acre in 2010 to $8,700 in 2013 with rents at 3-6.5% of value and barely moving year to year, whereas randomly picked stocks (Park Electrochemical, Premier Gold Mines, a Singapore nano-cap) showed 68% to 5x swings in 52-week ranges.

ideas.idea: A whole-market selloff marks down businesses whose value did not change at all, which a private seller would never accept.
ideas.detail: Service Corp, the funeral-services company, fell 2% on a day the Dow dropped 300 points and fell sharply in 2008-09 even though human mortality did not change; a private funeral home seller would tell a buyer demanding a 2% cut to take a hike.

ideas.idea: Buffett's inner scorecard means marching to your own drummer and not caring what the world thinks, which is essential because value investments are usually cheap for a reason many people believe and require contrarian conviction.
ideas.detail: At their lunch Buffett asked whether you would rather be the world's best lover but known as the worst, or the worst but known as the best; Pabrai exit-interviewed everyone afterwards and counted about 54 topics covered over three hours.

ideas.idea: Rick Guerin's story shows that leverage and being in a hurry can wipe out even a brilliant investor; if you are slightly above average and spend less than you earn you cannot help but get wealthy over a lifetime.
ideas.detail: Guerin was levered into the 1973-74 crash, got margin calls and had to sell his Berkshire shares to Buffett at about $40; Buffett said 'Charlie and I always knew we were going to get very rich, but we weren't in a hurry. Rick was in a hurry.'

ideas.idea: The number one skill in investing is extreme patience; the Fidelity accounts that performed best were those whose owners had forgotten they existed.
ideas.detail: Real business change happens over years, not days or weeks; he admits only one stock in his portfolio is more than three years old and that his portfolio would do incredibly well if he simply went away for 10 years.

ideas.idea: Always choose truth over diplomacy even when it causes near-term pain, because trust compounds and small lies erode it.
ideas.detail: Drawing on David Hawkins' 'Power vs. Force', he told investors candidly in 2008 that the fund's 67% drop was partly his own mistakes, not just the crisis, and redemptions were benign because investors trusted him; Buffett likewise starts annual reports with mistakes and tells managers 'give me the bad news first'.

ideas.idea: Design your environment to discourage activity: no Bloomberg, no team, trades after hours, no discussion of current positions with investors, and many non-investing pursuits.
ideas.detail: Discussing positions publicly creates commitment and consistency bias that makes it hard to sell when wrong; he plays bridge 4-5 hours a week, racquetball and biking, and only acts when an idea is a total no-brainer.

ideas.idea: The world misprices the talent of stay-at-home moms; Pabrai Funds runs entirely on part-time staff at under $100,000 a year of payroll on $700 million of assets.
ideas.detail: His part-time staff handle everything including SEC compliance; he also says running his earlier IT services company taught him more about operating businesses than running a fund does.

ideas.idea: When looking at a stock, look for a reason to say no as fast as possible: first is it in the circle of competence, second is it super cheap, then spend 30 minutes hunting for a showstopper before going deeper.
ideas.detail: There are 25-50,000 stocks worldwide and a serious look takes weeks, so you could cover at most 50 a year; you need shortcuts that eliminate most of the universe quickly.

ideas.idea: Cloning 13Fs is like bowling with bumpers: focus on the top three to five positions of great investors, because those ideas have already passed through a good filter.
ideas.detail: Looking only at the top five positions of Einhorn, Ackman, Icahn, Buffett and Klarman gives a pond of under 100 stocks a year, and the 30th position of a manager is not going to help you much.

ideas.idea: 'Unknown upside without downside' is a powerful mental model because markets are very bad at pricing uncertainty.
ideas.detail: His fund's first investment in 1999 was Silicon Valley Bank, a conservatively run bank at a small premium to book that held an undisclosed basket of warrants in dot-com startups; the stock doubled quickly and he exited. Earlier, in 1995, he made 100x on CMGI bought at a small premium to cash, though in hindsight he should have sold at 5x.

ideas.idea: A great operator can make a fully priced business not fully priced; the 3G team can squeeze blood out of a rock.
ideas.detail: If you understand what 3G did at Burger King and AB InBev and is likely to do at Kraft and Tim Hortons, you can assume they will extract more margin than historical levels even with a stagnant top line.

ideas.idea: The target is close to a 100% probability of at least 2x in two years with near-zero chance of anything else; the probability of a permanent loss of capital should be under 1%.
ideas.detail: He dismisses his own book's probability framing as 'stupid': losing 0-30% should be under 1% probability, losing more than 30% should approach zero, returns between 1x and 2x under 10%, and above 2x the rest.

ideas.idea: If you are questioning whether something is in your circle of competence, it is not; operate dead center of the circle, not near the edges.
ideas.detail: John Arrillaga only buys real estate within two miles of Stanford and can answer the competence question in three seconds; Pabrai will not invest unless he can nail the thesis in three sentences. The circle grows by osmosis over a lifetime, especially each time you lose money, so focus on staying inside it rather than expanding it.

ideas.idea: Ignore currencies and do not hedge; if the business thesis works out, currency moves should not matter much, and closer to home you understand more.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Hedging is expensive and he has no view on currencies; going global carries risks locals would spot, but no-brainers abroad are still worth pursuing. In late 2014 he found little to buy in the US and his current idea was outside the US.

ideas.idea: In private deals with intelligent sellers you should expect to pay a full price, but small growing private businesses can still return 5-10x in five to seven years, unlike sub-$50 million public 'zombie' companies burdened by public-company overhead.
ideas.detail: Low interest rates depress insurance company valuations, making it a good time to hunt; Dhandho can add value by improving the investment portfolio of an insurer that sits entirely in fixed income.

ideas.idea: Berkshire is a reasonable holding near Buffett's buyback floor of 1.2x book, but with small capital you ought to find things that do better than Berkshire, Fairfax or Leucadia.
ideas.detail: Allan Mecham of Arlington held over 50% in Berkshire and levered it against the buyback floor, but Pabrai notes Buffett would not defend the floor in a 2009-type scenario, recalling Rick Guerin; Fairfax targets 15% long-term returns and Leucadia must be re-handicapped now that the founders are gone.

ideas.idea: The long-term strategic plan for Pabrai Funds is simply to avoid stupid decisions and make as few decisions as possible.
ideas.detail: If he were not managing the fund he would return the capital; he does not consider it work and reads about 100-150 pages a day versus Buffett's reported 500.

ideas.idea: For a cheap, growing business you do not need to agonize over the exit multiple; if earnings compound as expected, any reasonable multiple gives a great result.
ideas.detail: Using a student's Jammu and Kashmir Bank at 6x earnings and near 1x book: a well-run Indian bank should grow at about 2x GDP, roughly 15% a year, so $100 million of earnings becomes $200 million in five years and a 10x, 15x or 20x multiple gives $2-4 billion versus a $600 million market cap; the real risk is only the loan book.

ideas.idea: The best investment is a company that is very cheap, has good growth prospects and generates high returns on capital, and the temperament required is to do nothing daily and act only when no spreadsheet is required.
ideas.detail: Jammu and Kashmir Bank is cheap because it is 53% state-owned in a militarized region hit by Srinagar floods, yet India issues almost no new bank licenses and Modi wants to bank the unbanked half of the country; he tells the student not to sell before October 8, 2024.

ideas.idea: Stay away from businesses in secular decline; owning them has attributes similar to shorting, and Buffett knows of zero successful retailer turnarounds.
ideas.detail: He lost money on Sears and learned that Eddie Lampert is a first-rate investor but a third-rate retailer; the people who shop at Sears are dying and no one born today will shop there, whereas Buffett's batting average is near perfect on banks and media but horrible on retailers.

ideas.idea: Recurring revenue is a concept you cannot give enough weight to; a bank keeps its customers for decades while a retailer must win each purchase anew.
ideas.detail: Banking relationships stay forever whereas retail stickiness, once in decline as at Sears, is almost impossible to reverse; Amazon is an example of a retailer with real stickiness.
